fixes.explanation: That's the one, friend. Amos says, "Woe to those at ease in Zion and those secure on Mount Samaria…" (Amos 6:1). These folks have settled in so deep they've got dents in the couch.
Nope, the text paints the opposite picture. Amos calls them "at ease" and "secure" (Amos 6:1). Afraid and on guard would be a very different verse.

Not quite, friend. Verse 1 says "at ease" and "secure" (Amos 6:1). Hungry and worn out isn't in the verse. Amos calls them the distinguished ones of the foremost nation, and the house of Israel comes to them.
That's right, friend. The text says they "…bring near a reign of violence." (Amos 6:3). So they dismiss the day of calamity and bring violence near. I think that's a rough trade.

You got it, baker. Amos says, "You dine on lambs from the flock and calves from the stall." (Amos 6:4). That's lamb and calf on the menu while they lounge on ivory beds. Nobody in this scene is eating over the sink.
Those sound tasty, but they're not on this table. Amos says they dine on "…lambs from the flock and calves from the stall." (Amos 6:4). Barley loaves and figs aren't in the verse.
Not this time, friend. Lentils and wild greens aren't in the verse. Amos says, "You dine on lambs from the flock and calves from the stall." (Amos 6:4). That's what's on their table.

That's right. Amos says, "You improvise songs on the harp like David and invent your own musical instruments." (Amos 6:5). They play the harp like David, and they invent instruments of their own. That's a lot of creativity, friend.

Actually, the text says they do. Amos puts it right after the harp: "…and invent your own musical instruments." (Amos 6:5). So they're not just playing like David, they're inventing instruments too. That makes True the answer.

Yes, grieve. Amos says they drink wine, anoint themselves with the finest oils, "…but you fail to grieve over the ruin of Joseph." (Amos 6:6). The wine and the oil sit in the same verse as the failure to grieve. Grief is the thing missing.

Right, and it's a hard turn. Amos says, "Therefore, you will now go into exile as the first of the captives, and your feasting and lounging will come to an end." (Amos 6:7). The ones who were lounging are named the first of the captives.
Not quite, friend. Amos says they will "…go into exile as the first of the captives…" (Amos 6:7). Soldiers aren't in the verse. The word Amos uses is captives.
That's not it, friend. The LORD says He abhors Jacob's pride and detests his citadels (Amos 6:8). Weakness isn't in the verse. The word He swears by Himself is pride.
Actually, the text says He does. The LORD declares, "…so I will deliver up the city and everything in it." (Amos 6:8). That includes everything in it, friend. So True is the answer.
Not quite, friend. The person inside answers, "None" (Amos 6:10). It's a short answer with a lot behind it. I think this is a heavy verse.

You got it. The LORD says, "But you have turned justice into poison and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood…" (Amos 6:12). That's two turnarounds in one verse, friend. Justice into poison, and the fruit of righteousness into wormwood.
Good try, but no. The LORD says, "But you have turned justice into poison…" (Amos 6:12). Feasts into fasting isn't what He says there. The charge is about justice and righteousness.
That's the one. They say, "Did we not take Karnaim by our own strength?" (Amos 6:13). Notice who gets the credit in that sentence. It's all "we" and "our own."
